paragraphs: October 21, 1991: Apple launches the Macintosh PowerBook 100 series. The lightweight Mac laptops will quickly become one of the most important tech gadgets of all time.

These devices will almost single-handedly turn notebook computers into mainstream technology. Apple’s subsequent success in this category — whether it’s current MacBooks or even the rise of mobile devices like the iPhone — owes a huge debt to the PowerBook 100 series.

Before the MacBook became the default laptop for creative professionals, Apple had to figure out how to make a computer genuinely portable. With the PowerBook 100, Apple didn’t just shrink the desktop Mac. It redefined what a computer could be when you took it out into the world.

It established the laptop design we still recognize today, with a keyboard pushed back from the front edge and a pointing device nestled below it. That formula proved wildly successful, helping turn portable computing into a common experience.

By modern standards, the PowerBook 100 series is the first true laptop Apple released. But it wasn’t the company’s first mobile computer. In September 1989, Apple launched the Macintosh Portable, a battery-powered Mac you could take on the go. The Macintosh Portable didn’t fare well, though. That probably shouldn’t seem too surprising, considering it cost $6,500 — and weighed 15.8 pounds!

By comparison, the PowerBooks came in three configurations when they launched two years later in October 1991: the low-end PowerBook 100, the midlevel PowerBook 140 and the high-end PowerBook 170. These ranged in price from $2,300 to $4,599. The PowerBook 100 notebooks weighed just 5.1 pounds, making them practical in a way the Mac Portable never had been.

The PowerBook 100 looked somewhat different from the PowerBook 140 and 170, for good reason. While Apple designed the latter two models, Sony designed the former. The PowerBook 100 shipped with 2MB of expandable RAM (up to 8MB) and a hard drive ranging from 20MB to 40MB.

Users wanting a floppy drive could buy an external one, although the peripheral shipped as standard with the two higher-end models. Only the top-end PowerBook 170 came with an active-matrix display. All three models featured a built-in trackball for controlling the cursor, which drew plenty of comments at the time.
